name: Diego Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers are confidential. What is a usual day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the crusher crew at Black Ridge mine and operate the feed loader when the belt backs up. My two-year technical diploma helps with faults, but I learned most of the sounds beside the machine. I am fifty-eight, my partner and I have grown children, and retirement is somewhere ahead. A long spell helping family left us with less than a month of expenses saved, despite my senior job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a quicker report is fine if it leaves the crusher checks with us. I have tried an AI summary a few times, but I still listen to the bearings. A screen does not hear a rattle through the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My role is senior, but my pay is at the low end for this work. One missed week would squeeze us, and there are few other mines nearby. I would feel relief about the machine, not about the household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep operating the feed loader and doing the morning bearing check. I would ask payroll for the exact balance of my pension this month and compare it with our weekly bills. I would take any spare shift rather than assume a mild AI story makes us safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money. Slower AI progress does not refill the savings account that family care costs emptied.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What payment would slip first after a missed week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The heating payment would be late before the food bill. I would call the provider and ask for two instalments. I do not want our grown children paying for our ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the AI summary help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It put three fault notes for the same bearing together. I checked them in the original log before showing the mechanic. I would use it again, but not as a substitute for listening.

say: I would accept **quicker reports** while keeping crusher checks with the crew.
I would keep **listening to bearings**, even when an AI summary makes notes shorter.
think: My **senior title** does not erase low pay or less than one month saved.
Few **nearby mines** make one lost week hard to replace.
do: **Keep** running the feed loader and checking crusher bearings each morning.
**Request** my pension balance and compare it with weekly household bills.
feel: **Anxious** about existing bills despite little AI change.
S0.quote: Slower AI progress does not refill the savings account that family care costs emptied.
fieldNote: His **seniority** and strong skill sit beside thin savings and lower pay.
He already uses AI **occasionally**, but listening to the crusher remains his main check.
The pension request is for **information**, not proof he can retire.

steps.text: Keep operating feed loader and checking crusher bearings
Request pension balance before making retirement plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say planning and parts orders may change before the crusher itself. The crew should see any AI maintenance schedule before it removes a checking shift. I would bring that point to our union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine saves office time, management may expect one person to cover two crusher checks. I am good at the job, but even I cannot be at both ends of the belt at once. Losing one of my own shifts would hit our bills immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new AI maintenance screen from the mechanic after she had used it for a month. I would log how long the physical checks take and take any cut in shift hours to the union steward. I would keep the crew on the old safety walk until a new schedule proved itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I might keep the lead title and still bring home less pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which check would be lost first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The late bearing walk is easy to erase from a neat schedule. I would show the steward last month’s fault log and the time it took. A title does not pay the heating bill if the shift disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for a different mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are only a couple within reach, and they may use the same schedule. I would first fight for the check to stay. I would apply elsewhere only if my hours actually fell.

say: I would bring **AI maintenance schedules** to the union before physical checks are cut.
I would keep the **late bearing walk** on the roster.
think: The mine might reduce **my hours** even if it keeps my crew lead title.
A lost shift would quickly strain **household bills**.
do: **Learn** the AI maintenance screen from the mechanic after her trial month.
**Log** physical check times and take lost hours to the union steward.
feel: **Anxious** about lower pay despite his senior title.
S1.quote: A title does not pay the heating bill if the shift disappears.
fieldNote: He sees **desk planning** change first but fears it will remove his own checking hours.
Learning waits until a **colleague tests** the screen, matching his cautious pace.
Union action follows a **documented loss** in checks or hours.

steps.text: Learn AI maintenance screen after mechanic tests it for one month
Take reduced check hours to union steward if roster shrinks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crusher crew that full thinking AI by 2028 changes schedules first, while capable loader robots appear around 2031. The mine might then buy them for the feed yard. We need paid training and income protection written down before that choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty when thinking AI arrives and sixty-three when capable robots follow. If Black Ridge replaced my loader shifts then, I could not live on our tiny savings. My partner’s part-time pay covers some food, not our whole home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop our planned trip to visit relatives and ask the union steward for an income protection proposal this month. I would take paid instruction on crusher inspection if the mine posted a real position. After 2028 I would keep operating the loader while people still do that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I would be awake adding up weeks of bills, because my title cannot buy the missing months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell the relatives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the trip has to wait until we know the mine’s plans. They would understand, though I would hate saying it. The travel money is one of the few amounts we can hold back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children support you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They could help once, but they have their own bills. I would ask the union for a wage bridge and the mine for real jobs first. I do not want our children turned into our pension.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AI** from capable feed-loader robots around 2031.
I would press for **income protection** and paid inspection training before driver posts go.
think: At **sixty-three** when capable robots appear, I could lose loader wages before affordable retirement.
Our **tiny savings** and my partner’s part-time pay could not cover the household for long.
do: **Stop** the planned family visit and retain travel money for bills.
**Ask** the union steward for an income protection proposal this month.
**Take** paid crusher inspection instruction if a real position is posted.
feel: **Alarmed** about losing wages with almost no cash cushion.
S2.quote: I do not want our children turned into our pension.
fieldNote: He separates the **2028 schedule** change from capable robots around 2031.
At sixty-three, losing a lower-paid but essential **wage** would overwhelm his thin cushion.
Training requires a **paid place** with an actual position.

steps.text: Stop planned trip to relatives and hold travel money for bills
Ask union steward for written income protection proposal
Take paid crusher inspection instruction if real position posted
Keep operating feed loader after 2028 while human shifts remain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years to thinking AI and about eight to capable loader robots gives the mine time to fund a second skill. I would ask the union to negotiate paid inspection places. The crew should get dates, not a promise to talk later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-three when planning changes in 2031 and about sixty-six when capable robots appear in 2034. I might make it to retirement, but our savings are so thin I would need the pension figures first. A paid inspection role could keep wages coming if the loader shifts went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enrol in the mine’s paid inspection course next year if a real opening was posted and my wages continued during class. I would request a pension forecast and review it with my partner. I would keep the physical crusher walk on the roster while I trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a possible route. Eight years matters if the mine pays us to prepare, not if it only gives us a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course need to cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bearing temperatures, belt alignment and how to stop a feed before it jams. I already know the sounds, but I would need formal inspection records. A certificate should lead to a paid inspection shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the opening never appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the loader wage and look at the pension forecast again. There are few mines nearby, so I would not borrow for a course without a post. I would ask the union to keep pressing for one.

say: I would ask the **union** to negotiate paid inspection places before capable robots around 2034.
I would demand **dated plans** for the crew.
think: At about **sixty-six** when robots become capable, affordable retirement is still uncertain.
A paid **inspection shift** could replace loader wages if a real post exists.
do: **Enrol** in paid inspection training if a real post opens and wages continue during class.
**Request** a pension forecast and compare it with household bills.
**Keep** the crusher safety walk on the roster while training.
feel: **Anxious**, with a possible paid route to another task.
S3.quote: A certificate should lead to a paid inspection shift.
fieldNote: He is **sixty-three** at thinking AI and about sixty-six when capable robots arrive.
His course decision depends on a **real opening** and wages continuing through training.
Thin savings mean a pension forecast is **necessary** before assuming retirement.

steps.text: Enrol in inspection course if post opens and wages continue
Request pension forecast before deciding retirement timing
Keep crusher safety walk while training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years to thinking AI and about thirteen to capable loader robots is useful warning if the mine keeps paying its crews. I would ask for a funded training timetable now. Younger workers should not reach 2039 without a real trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-eight in 2036 and about seventy-one when capable robots arrive in 2039. I hope to have retired, but less than one month saved today makes that a hope, not a plan. The pension forecast and steady shifts matter more to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the crusher crew while my health and shifts allow it. I would ask the pension office for a forecast this year and sit with my partner over the weekly budget. I would help the union draft a funded training plan for younger operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about retirement income, even with robots far away. A decade of wages would help only if the shifts actually stayed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you set a retirement date now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the pension and bills must be compared first. My partner and I would decide together after seeing the forecast. I cannot name an age just because a technology card names a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for the younger operators?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid technical courses and time beside experienced mechanics. I would put that in a union proposal, not just tell them to be flexible. A young worker cannot eat a promise of future jobs.

say: I would ask for a **funded timetable** while the mine has years to prepare.
I would bring **younger operators** into the union training proposal.
think: At about **seventy-one** when capable robots arrive, I hope to have retired but cannot assume it.
Today’s **thin savings** make steady shifts and a pension forecast essential.
do: **Keep** leading crusher shifts while work and health allow.
**Request** a pension forecast and compare it with weekly bills.
**Help** the union draft paid technical training for younger operators.
feel: **Anxious** about retirement income despite the distant robot date.
S4.quote: A young worker cannot eat a promise of future jobs.
fieldNote: The **2039 robot date** may follow retirement, but his funding is still uncertain.
He favours **collective training** for younger operators rather than general encouragement.
His household relies on **continued wages** during the long warning.

steps.text: Keep leading Black Ridge crusher shifts while able
Request pension forecast before setting retirement date
Help union draft funded technical training plan

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable loader robots could arrive around 2031 before I can afford retirement. Paid inspection training tied to real posts and a wage bridge would help. The union needs to put both in writing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask why a lead worker can still have so little saved. Family care took years of our money, and my pay is low for this job. I can hear a crusher fault through the floor, but that skill cannot pay a bill after the shift disappears.

headlineQuote: I can hear a crusher fault through the floor, but that skill cannot pay a bill after the shift disappears.
portrait: Diego Farah is a **58-year-old** crusher crew lead at Black Ridge mine, with a technical diploma and grown children.
Family care left him with **thin savings** despite senior skill; lower pay and few nearby mines make missed shifts serious.
He tries **AI after colleagues** and uses logs and union meetings to protect checks and hours.
Fast robot availability makes him **alarmed** about wages; longer warning helps only with funded training and continued shifts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because capable feed-loader robots could arrive around 2031 before he can afford retirement.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid inspection training** tied to real posts and a written wage bridge would help him plan for possible lost shifts.
